title: 🎙️ Science, Wonder & the Natural World
description: Today we look at scientific discovery and the natural world — from ecology and wildlife research to astronomy and deep-sea biology. We're grounding these stories in the landscapes and living systems of the Cariboo: what salmon runs, boreal forest research, or species-at-risk studies tell us about the wild places we live beside. We're after stories that inspire curiosity and wonder about how the world works. - Daily themed article selection for podcast generation

_podcast.theme_description: Today we look at scientific discovery and the natural world — from ecology and wildlife research to astronomy and deep-sea biology. We're grounding these stories in the landscapes and living systems of the Cariboo: what salmon runs, boreal forest research, or species-at-risk studies tell us about the wild places we live beside. _podcast.theme_scoring_prompt: Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Science, Wonder & the Natural World' — scientific discovery, ecology, natural phenomena, and the curiosity-driven study of living systems. Strong fits include: wildlife biology and species research, ecology studies and biodiversity findings, watershed and salmon research relevant to BC, astronomy and space science, new species discoveries, citizen science projects, natural history stories, wildfire science and forest ecology, climate science findings (not just policy), geology, evolution, and deep-time Earth stories, and any scientific research grounded in BC or Cariboo landscapes and ecosystems. Prefer articles that convey genuine curiosity and discovery — the 'how' and 'why' of the natural world. Score 70–90 for: prehistoric life and palaeontology (ancient oceans, Cretaceous ecology, deep-time species), new species discoveries in ocean or remote environments, deep-sea biology, evolutionary biology findings, natural history stories with a strong sense of wonder, and field research grounded in BC ecosystems. Penalise (score 0–30): consumer health and pharmaceutical research without ecology or natural-world context; pure policy and advocacy news; technology business stories without a science or ecology angle; human interest and viral news without scientific substance; geopolitical and crime news. Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.title: [phys.org] Fire amoeba breaks complex-life heat tolerance record at 63°C
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Scientists have identified a new amoeba, Incendiamoeba cascadensis, that can eat, move and reproduce in water as hot as 63°C (145°F) at California’s Lassen Volcanic National Park, setting a record for the highest temperature known to support eukaryotic reproduction. The NASA-supported study, published in Cell on Sept. 22, found that the organism remains active at about 64°C and can recover after five minutes at 70°C, although exposure to 80°C proved fatal [phys.org#1][nasa.gov#1][livescience.com#1][sciencenews.org#1]. The finding challenges the previous 60°C upper limit for eukaryotic growth and reproduction, based on the heat sensitivity of proteins and other complex cellular structures. Researchers said the amoeba withstands the heat by changing shape and forming a protective outer layer; genetic analysis also identified genes associated with repairing heat-damaged proteins [nasa.gov#1][science.org#1][orf.at#1]. The work is relevant to astrobiology because scientists use extreme environments on Earth to assess where complex life might survive on Mars and other worlds [nasa.gov#1][npr.org#1].

items.title: [ScienceDaily] These tropical trees breathe at night to survive drought
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Some tropical trees have evolved a clever way to survive drought by taking in carbon dioxide at night, allowing them to keep their pores closed during the hot daytime and conserve water. By comparing three Clusia species, researchers discovered that this water-saving form of photosynthesis, known as CAM, did not arise through a single evolutionary change. Instead, ancient genome duplications followed by millions of years of genetic reshuffling produced strikingly different strategies, from strong CAM to stress-triggered and hybrid forms.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists opened a sealed envelope after 10 years. Gravity still didn’t make sense
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

A decade-long NIST experiment has produced a new measurement of the universal gravitational constant that differs unexpectedly from another leading result, deepening a 225-year-old physics puzzle. The discrepancy is tiny, but for one of nature’s most fundamental constants, it is large enough to keep scientists wondering whether hidden experimental errors or something more surprising is involved.
